newsitem.title: USA: EPA should curb medical waste burners, report says.
newsitem.headline: EPA should curb medical waste burners, report says.

text.p: Hospitals should be forced to drastically cut back incineration of their waste that is a major producer of highly toxic dioxin, environmental advocates said Thursday.

With the Environmental Protection Agency set to issue a final rule in July on medical waste disposal, an environmental group in a report said the agency appeared to be "poised to capitulate" to the American Hospital Association, which wants to avoid stricter rules.

The Environmental Working Group in its report said the EPA's proposal "would allow hundreds of medwaste incinerators to continue operation with no pollution control equipment whatsoever," and urged the EPA to strengthen the measures before the final rule is issued in July.

Burning of large numbers of plastic materials used in hospitals, such as polyvinyl gloves and intravenous feeding bags, make medical waste incinerators a major producer of emissions of dioxin, a toxic waste product that can cause cancer and disrupt human and animal endocrine systems.
Medical waste burners also may emit mercury and other hazardous substances, the group said.
To dispose of the relatively small amount of infectious wastes they produce, the report said hospitals burn far more waste than they need to.
The report urged that hospitals eliminate non-essential incineration and switch to substitutes when possible for polyvinyl plastics and other plastics that produce dioxin when burned.

It said the EPA should hold medical waste incinerators to the same standard as other hazardous waste burners, hold rural hospital incinerators to the same standards as urban, and improve public information on medical waste incineration.
EPA's plan for large medical waste burners is "ten times weaker than that proposed for hazardous waste incinerators, cement kilns and other burners," the report said.
The Environmental Working Group complained that the EPA backed off its initial proposed rule, and offered "revisions" that it said significantly weakened the plan.

In its proposed revisions, the EPA narrowed the definition of medical waste, eased standards for small incinerators, and loosened requirements for monitoring, inspecting and compliance testing for facilities.
The American Hospital Association "overall is supportive of the new proposal," spokeswoman Alicia Mitchell said.
Mitchell said a number of hospitals are trying to reduce their waste incineration, increase recycling and use substitutes for chlorinated plastics when possible.
But she said such measures add costs.
"We want to make sure that we are protecting the public, but spending health care dollars in a responsible way as well," Mitchell said.
